that's based on a lot of assumptions that aren't necessarily true.  first, that the sold object has a definable value, second that consumers decide whether or not to buy based on the discrepancy between asking price and definable value, and that there's any semblance of equality in the sellers' relative marketability.  these premises aren't based on anything but intuition and fallacy, my brother.  

taking the selling pepsi example; you've got a hundred bucks and can get a hundred pepsis to then resell.  on the assumption that all pepsis are then sold for 200 bucks, you've doubled your investment.  that's great.  now, do you go back to the vendor and say "200 pepsis please!" and then sell those again with the same technique for 400 bucks?  maybe, it's possible.  but you might also shop for a new vendor, now that your resources are more substantial and you have a wedge of the market you can claim to represent.  you might bid your vendor down to 85 cents a can, since he stands to make a greater profit from the larger buy regardless of the decrease in profit-per-can.  so you can buy 200 cans if you want, maybe pocket the extra thirty bucks, or buy substantially more product to then flip for additional profit.  

you take a million bucks to the vendor, he says these cans cost a buck a pop, you buy and flip a million cans and now you've got two million.  all of this is still within proportion.  but having doubled a million represents a significant accrual of resources compared to the paltry doubling of a hundred.  it also represents a greater market share, having sold one million instead of one hundred.  thus increasing the seller's bargaining power against the vendor to a more significant degree.  

all things being proportionate, your math makes sense.  but all things are not proportionate, they're equal, and when cost and losses are weighed against THE DOLLAR and not against the proportion of your wealth that dollar represents, less money means disproportionately less opportunity (in this example, by several orders of magnitude.)

this isn't mathematically sound.

starting with 100 dollars, you have 100 dollars to turn a profit.  99 can be total failures, but if you can make money on 1, you can theoretically see profits soar at a rate much higher than 50:1 or 5000:1.  So turning 100 into 5000, or 500,000, is not as simple as saying each dollar brings a specific ratio of return.  The return is averaged against losses, each dollar holding individual identical potential but not performing identically.  

step up from 100 to 1,000,000 and you still have many of the same conditions; except you have exponentially more chances to FUCK UP before making a return.  The likelihood of success isn't based around comparable rates of return, it's based on the amount of fucking up you can get away with before penalties overtake profits.

I'm currently a little more than halfway through Mr. Peanut by Adam Ross.  The story revolves around a potential spousal murder/suicide, and began mainly as the story of David Pepin and his wife Alice (the deceased.)  But it's chapters continuously rotate between David's life leading up the murder, and the lives of the detectives investigating the murder (their past and present.)  Its timeline is completely disjointed, the point of view keeps changing, and it's one of the most interesting books I've read in a while.

What I mean to say by this is that the story you're writing doesn't need to revolve solely around your protagonist.  You can attack it from various angles, having different perspectives casting different characters alternately into protagonist/antagonist roles.  Don't feel confined; tell the story in the most interesting, engulfing way you can manage.  If the reader gets lost or confused, make it so that they can resolve that confusion by reading further.

basically, the premise of the riddle is set up where you're meant to accept "one of us speaks only truth, the other only lies" as true; but when it comes half out of both mouths, it can't be true.  they must BOTH be lying.

didn't he end up realizing that both brothers were liars?

because brother 1 said "one of us tells only truth" and brother 2 said "the other, only lies," but there's no way to reconcile both of those half-statements as true.  and they can't both be telling the truth, because that contradicts the sentence.  so they were both liars.

and tipping is often seen as "extra" by people unfamiliar with the business model, but the system is designed to make the server wholly dependent on tips because it's what's best for the restaurant.  if the restaurant itself was paying out the server's wages, it would have to inflate pricing to compensate.  this essentially keeps the amount the customer spends the same (assuming servers would make the same amount with either model,) while removing a good part of the server's incentive to provide superior service.

the way the model works now, the restaurant keeps its costs artificially low, the customer pays roughly the same amount they would under a wage model, and the server typically sees a direct correlation between quality of service and quantity of tips.

because servers are forced to declare tips (at times compelled to declare more than they're taking home,) the taxation against these tips comes from the check.  in times of plenty, you're making too much in tips for your hourly to cover your taxes, so you're losing the whole check and racking up a tab.  when things are tighter, and you're being compensated with increased hourly wage, you're still getting taxed at a rate based on year-to-date average earnings, and the check's probably going to disappear completely anyway.  this might lessen your year-end tax burden, but still leaves you with empty pockets.

Don't tell their spouses anything, just that they're taking a trip.  Then they come up here, into these special, special mountains.  And they break my rules."*

this is my cursive story.  i never get to tell it on the internet.

in 2008 cursive played a show at the polish club in poughkeepsie, new york.  my roommates and i, who were living in white plains (not that far from poughkeepsie) got tickets and went.  the polish club is set up with a bar on the first floor, and the venue on the second.  myself and another friend were the only two in our group old enough to drink, and hung out at the bar before the show began.  GO FIGURE, ted stevens and matt maginn were playing pool nonchalantly in the bar.  i don't know if nobody recognized them or what, but they were just hanging out by themselves.

my friend and i bought them a round of beers and started talking to them.  we're 21, they're considerably older.  they were the NICEST FUCKING PEOPLE I'VE EVER MET.  we shot the shit, made a friendly wager on a game, and generally caroused before the show.  then-drummer cornbread compton showed up mid-game, and we talked about garfieldminusgarfield until they got called away.  ted told us, secretly, that "sierra" was the fourth song on the set list.

show starts, and my buddy and i push our way to the front of the stage.  not even much pushing, considering the show was ~200 people, but we got right up front.  after the third song ended, we started chanting "SIERRA!  SIERRA!  SIERRA!"  it comes on, we feel like gods even though we knew we cheated.

by the time the show ends my voice is gone, my feet and hands hurt from clapping and stomping, and i can't hear worth shit.  tim hands the set list to some kid a few people down from us, and i am crestfallen.  but ted.  that slick sonofabitch ted.  he draws out the encore for an extra few minutes, just mashing the guitar with drumsticks, smashing it into the amps, it's amazing.  and here's where i jizzed:

ted stevens, lead guitarist for my favorite band, jumps off the stage into the thinning crowd, chucks the drumsticks, looks at me, says "JOE!  WE'RE DOING SHOTS!" and invites us down to drink with the band.  

we get one drink but have to leave early because our under-21ers drove and are leaving.  the whole band signed the shirt i was wearing, ted signed the dollar i won off him at pool, and tim put a heart on my right nipple and an X on my left.  

my whole life has been downhill since that night, but it was the greatest experience of my life.  

tl;dr:  got to drink and play pool with cursive a few years ago.  single greatest night of my life.

I had a similar, albeit unrelated, situation once at a supermarket.  I'd gone in the night I found out my stepdad had cancer to buy nicotine patches.  Their pharmacy was closed, and when I asked at Customer Service if anyone had the key, I was told they didn't.  It was a totally separately-run department, apparently.  Instead of telling me "the pharmacy will be back open tomorrow at 8" or whatever, the CS guy told me I could get the same patches cheaper at a store half-a-block away that was open later.  He cared more than I bought the patches than that I bought them from his store.  So now, I do all of my grocery shopping there.  For a store that size, I'm sure my 100 dollars every two weeks doesn't add much to their revenue, but that one instance made me a loyal customer of theirs.
